Correct answer: B. Cuneiform cataract

Ans. B) Cuneiform cataract

 

Cuneiform (cortical) cataract begins as wedge-shaped opacities in the lens cortex, typically starting peripherally and moving inward. Patients mainly complain of poor vision in dim light because the dilated pupil allows light to pass through the opaque peripheral lens. It is not associated with difficulty seeing in bright light. Instead, patients often report night glare and haloes.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Nuclear cataract: Affects the central nucleus of the lens. Causes difficulty in bright light due to increased light scatter and glare. Patients may notice a temporary improvement in near vision (“second sight”), but distant vision worsens in sunlight.

 

Option C. Posterior subcapsular cataract: Opacity lies just in front of the posterior capsule. Vision becomes worse in bright light and while reading, because pupil constriction directs light through the cloudy posterior area. Common in diabetics and those on steroids.

 

Option D. Steroid-induced cataract: Typically a posterior subcapsular variety. Produces photophobia and glare in bright light, similar to idiopathic posterior subcapsular cataract.

questions.text: The most common cause of p‍roptosis in middle-aged i​ndividuals is:
questions.raw_text: The most common cause of proptosis in middle-aged individuals is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Thyroid eye disease

Ans. C) Thyroid eye disease

 

Thyroid eye disease (TED) — also called Graves’ ophthalmopathy or thyroid-associated orbitopathy — is the most common cause of proptosis in middle-aged adults.

 

It is an autoimmune inflammatory disorder in which activated T-lymphocytes target orbital fibroblasts and pre-adipocytes, leading to:

 

  • Enlargement of extraocular muscles (classically sparing tendinous insertions)
  • Increased orbital fat and connective tissue
  • Resultant axial proptosis (bilateral or unilateral)

 

Typical features:

 

  • Lid retraction (“stare” appearance)
  • Periorbital edema, conjunctival chemosis
  • Diplopia (due to extraocular muscle restriction)
  • Exposure keratopathy
  • Optic neuropathy (in severe cases)

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Cavernous hemangioma:

 

  • Most common benign orbital tumor in adults, but causes slowly progressive unilateral proptosis rather than bilateral or fluctuating proptosis.
  • Typically seen in women, located within the intraconal space, and not inflammatory in nature.
  • Hence, it is a cause of proptosis but not the most common overall.

 

Option B. Orbital varix:

 

  • A venous malformation leading to intermittent, positional proptosis (worsens on bending forward or straining).
  • Seen in younger adults, less common than thyroid orbitopathy.

 

Option D. Retinoblastoma:

 

  • Malignant retinal tumor occurring in children, not middle-aged individuals.
  • Proptosis in retinoblastoma is secondary to orbital extension of the tumor, not primary orbital pathology.

questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Krukenberg spindle

Ans. A) Krukenberg spindle

 

Krukenberg spindle is not a feature of complicated cataract.
It refers to a vertical, spindle-shaped deposit of pigment on the posterior surface of the cornea (endothelium), typically seen in pigment dispersion syndrome or pigmentary glaucoma, not in cataracts.

 

The pigment originates from the posterior surface of the iris and gets deposited on the corneal endothelium due to aqueous convection currents.

 

Thus, while it’s an ophthalmic finding, it is unrelated to complicated cataract formation.

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Polychromatic lustre: Seen in complicated cataracts, where the lens shows multicolored reflexes when illuminated due to changes in refractive index of degenerating lens fibers. This iridescent appearance is a hallmark of chronic inflammatory cataract.

 

 

Option C. Occurs after uveitis: Complicated cataract develops secondary to chronic intraocular inflammation, especially anterior uveitis, iridocyclitis, or retinitis. Inflammation alters lens metabolism leading to opacification — hence, this is a classic cause.

 

Option D. Breadcrumb appearance: Refers to irregular, grayish-white opacities in the posterior subcapsular region of the lens — characteristic of complicated cataract due to inflammatory deposits resembling “bread crumbs.”

questions.raw_text: A 62-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department because of acute chest pain. Her blood pressure is 90/60 mm Hg and pulse is 42/min. An ECG reveals ST-segment elevation in the inferior leads. The appropriate therapy is initiated, including a medication to treat her bradycardia. After initial treatment, her blood pressure is 120/70 mm Hg and pulse is 76/min. However, she now complains of severe right-sided eye pain. Which of the following is the most likely cause for this patient's eye pain?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Glaucoma

Ans. D) Glaucoma

 

Clinical summary:

 

  • Elderly woman with inferior wall myocardial infarction (ST elevation in inferior leads)
  • Bradycardia (pulse 42/min) initially → treated → HR improved
  • Now develops acute severe right-sided eye pain

 

This sequence points toward acute angle-closure glaucoma caused by atropine, a drug commonly used to treat bradycardia in inferior MI.

 

Mechanism:

 

  • Inferior wall MI often involves the right coronary artery, which supplies the SA and AV nodes, leading to sinus bradycardia or AV block.
  • Treatment: Atropine, a muscarinic (M2) receptor antagonist, increases heart rate by blocking vagal tone.

 

However, atropine also blocks M3 receptors in the eye, causing:

 

  • Mydriasis (pupil dilation) → narrows the iridocorneal angle → obstructs aqueous humor outflow → sudden rise in intraocular pressure.
    → Result: Acute angle-closure glaucoma

 

Symptoms:

 

  • Sudden severe eye pain
  • Blurred vision, haloes around lights
  • Mid-dilated, non-reactive pupil
  • Corneal haze and redness
  • Often accompanied by nausea and vomiting

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Iridocyclitis (anterior uveitis):

 

  • Causes dull ocular pain and photophobia, not sudden severe pain.
  • Pupil is constricted (not dilated), and vision loss is gradual.
  • Not drug-induced.

 

Option B. Retinal artery thrombosis:

 

  • Painless, sudden loss of vision (“curtain coming down”).
  • No eye pain or redness.
  • Fundoscopy shows “cherry-red spot”.

 

Option C. Acute conjunctivitis:

 

  • Causes mild irritation, redness, tearing, and discharge.
  • No severe pain or vision loss.

questions.raw_text: A 65-year-old male complains of painless bilateral visual difficulty that has progressed over the last year. Fundoscopy is shown.  Which of the following would you expect most on visual field examination?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Central scotomas

Ans. C) Central scotomas

 

The fundus image shows age-related macular degeneration (ARMD) — a degenerative disease affecting the macula (central retina), responsible for detailed central vision.

 

The macula contains a high density of cone photoreceptors vital for fine visual acuity, color perception, and reading vision.
When it degenerates, central vision is lost, while peripheral vision remains intact, leading to central scotomas on visual field testing.

 

Key Fundus Findings in ARMD:

 

  • Drusen deposits (yellowish spots) in the macular area — extracellular material between Bruch’s membrane and the retinal pigment epithelium.
  • Retinal pigment epithelial changes (mottling or atrophy).
  • May progress to geographic atrophy (dry ARMD) or choroidal neovascularization with hemorrhage/exudate (wet ARMD).

 

Symptoms:

 

  • Painless, gradual central vision loss
  • Metamorphopsia (distorted vision)
  • Difficulty reading, recognizing faces

 

Other Options Explained:

 

Option A. Bitemporal hemianopsia: 

 

  • Caused by optic chiasm compression (e.g., pituitary adenoma).
  • Produces loss of temporal visual fields in both eyes, not central vision loss.

 

Option B. Arcuate scotomas: 

 

  • Seen in glaucoma due to optic nerve damage.
  • Visual loss follows the arcuate nerve fiber pattern in the mid-periphery, sparing the central field initially.

 

Option D. Macular sparing: 

 

  • Occurs in occipital lobe infarcts (posterior cerebral artery occlusion).
  • The macular area is spared due to dual blood supply from the middle cerebral artery, hence peripheral vision loss but preserved central vision — opposite of this case.

  • Horizontal lid laxity
  • Attenuation of lower lid retractors
  • Medial or lateral canthal tendon laxity

 

Surgical correction therefore focuses on tightening and repositioning of these structures.

questions.text: Which of the following is ‍supplied by contralateral​ nerve nuclei?
questions.raw_text: Which of the following is supplied by contralateral nerve nuclei?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Superior rectus

Ans. A) Superior rectus

 

Among all the extraocular muscles supplied by the oculomotor nerve (cranial nerve III), the superior rectus muscle is unique — it receives fibers from the contralateral oculomotor nucleus.

 

That means:

 

  • The right superior rectus is supplied by the left oculomotor nucleus,
  • And the left superior rectus by the right oculomotor nucleus.

 

This crossed innervation occurs because of the decussation of oculomotor fibers within the midbrain before they reach the muscle.

 

Functional Summary:

 

  • Action of superior rectus: Elevation, adduction, and intorsion of the eyeball.
  • The muscle originates from the common tendinous ring and inserts on the superior aspect of the sclera.
  • Its nerve supply comes from the opposite (contralateral) oculomotor nucleus — a key anatomical distinction.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Inferior rectus:

 

  • Supplied by the ipsilateral oculomotor nucleus.
  • Functions: Depression, adduction, and extorsion of the eye.

 

Option C. Medial rectus:

 

  • Supplied by the ipsilateral oculomotor nucleus.
  • Function: Adduction of the eyeball.

 

Option D. Inferior oblique:

 

  • Supplied by the ipsilateral oculomotor nucleus.
  • Functions: Elevation, abduction, and extorsion of the eye.

questions.text: A patient came from a fact‍ory with a chemical injur​y to the eye a few hours ‌back. Which is the first ​step in the management?
questions.raw_text: A patient came from a factory with a chemical injury to the eye a few hours back. Which is the first step in the management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Copious irrigation of eyes

Ans. C) Copious irrigation of eyes

 

In a patient with chemical injury to the eye, the first and most critical step is immediate and copious irrigation of the affected eye — even before taking history or assessing vision.

 

The goal is to remove or dilute the chemical agent as quickly as possible to prevent further penetration and damage to ocular tissues.

 

Why Irrigation Is the First Step:

 

  • Every second counts — the severity of ocular injury depends on contact time of the chemical with the cornea and conjunctiva.
  • Early and thorough irrigation can dramatically reduce long-term damage like corneal scarring, symblepharon, or vision loss.
  • Irrigation should continue until the ocular surface pH normalizes (checked with litmus paper or pH strips).

 

Ideal method:

 

  • Use normal saline, Ringer’s lactate, or even clean tap water if nothing else is available.
  • Eyelids should be everted to wash out trapped particles.
  • Irrigation is continued for at least 30 minutes or until pH = 7.0–7.4.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. IOP measurement: Inappropriate as an initial step. Measuring intraocular pressure is delayed until after irrigation and stabilization, as early tonometry may worsen corneal damage or contamination.

 

Option B. Visual acuity: Assessment of visual acuity is important but not before irrigation. Immediate vision testing wastes critical time when chemical damage is ongoing.

 

Option D. Take history: History (chemical type, exposure duration) is important after irrigation. During the acute stage, the focus is on neutralizing and flushing the chemical.

The image and history are classical of rhegmatogenous retinal detachment (RRD) — the most common type of retinal detachment.

 

Key clues from the question:

 

  • Sudden, painless visual loss described as a “veil” or “curtain” → typical of retinal detachment.
  • History of myopia → predisposes to peripheral retinal breaks or lattice degeneration.
  • History of cataract surgery (pseudophakia) → another important risk factor.
  • Ophthalmoscopic finding: Presence of tobacco dust (Shafer’s sign) — pigmented cells floating in the vitreous, indicating a retinal break and release of pigment from the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE).

 

Pathophysiology:

 

In rhegmatogenous retinal detachment, a break or tear in the retina allows liquefied vitreous humor to enter the subretinal space, separating the neurosensory retina from the RPE layer.

 

Common risk factors:

 

  • Myopia
  • Posterior vitreous detachment (age-related)
  • Ocular trauma
  • Previous intraocular surgery (especially cataract extraction)

 

Symptoms:

 

  • Sudden onset of flashes and floaters
  • “Curtain or veil” descending over visual field
  • No pain or redness

Option A. Breaks in Descemet’s membrane: Seen in corneal conditions such as Keratoconus (Vogt’s striae) or birth trauma (Haab’s striae) in congenital glaucoma. Not related to retinal pathology.

Fundus shows smooth dome-shaped elevation; Shafer’s sign is absent.

 

Option C. Tractional retinal detachment: Occurs from fibrovascular membranes pulling the retina off (e.g., diabetic retinopathy, retinopathy of prematurity). Gradual, non-rhegmatogenous, and non-sudden in onset.

He was previously started on antiretroviral therapy but has been noncompliant with his prescribed medications. Funduscopy reveals the findings seen in the image below. Which of the following medications is the best initial therapy for this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Ganciclovir

Ans. D) Ganciclovir

 

The fundus image shows fluffy yellow-white retinal lesions with hemorrhagic borders — the classic “pizza pie” or “cottage cheese with ketchup” appearance, diagnostic of Cytomegalovirus (CMV) retinitis.

 

This is the most common ocular opportunistic infection in AIDS patients with CD4 counts <50 cells/mm³.

 

Key features of CMV retinitis:

 

Etiology:


Reactivation of latent Cytomegalovirus (CMV) infection in immunocompromised individuals (particularly AIDS patients).

 

Clinical presentation:

 

  • Painless, progressive visual loss
  • Floaters and blurred vision
  • Often bilateral, but may start in one eye
  • No eye pain or redness (helps differentiate from HSV or VZV retinitis)

 

Fundus findings:

 

  • Retinal necrosis with hemorrhage and exudates (gives “pizza pie” or “cheese and ketchup” appearance)
  • Involvement typically starts in the posterior pole and may spread peripherally.

 

Treatment:

 

First-line therapy:


→ Ganciclovir (IV or oral) or Valganciclovir (oral prodrug)

 

Alternative / adjunct options:

 

  • Foscarnet or Cidofovir (for ganciclovir-resistant cases)
  • Intravitreal ganciclovir or foscarnet for severe sight-threatening lesions
  • Resume or initiate antiretroviral therapy (ART) to restore immune function.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Acyclovir: Used for HSV and VZV infections, not effective against CMV.

 

Option B. Amphotericin B: Used for fungal infections (e.g., Candida, Aspergillus, Cryptococcus), not viral infections.

 

Option C. Clarithromycin: Used for Mycobacterium avium complex (MAC) infections in AIDS, not for CMV.

Correct answer: C. Intravenous Acetazolamide, and Nd:YAG 1064nm laser Iridotomy

Ans. C) Intravenous Acetazolamide, and Nd:YAG 1064nm laser Iridotomy

 

This is a classic presentation of acute angle-closure glaucoma (AACG) — an ophthalmic emergency.

 

Step 1  Identifying the Diagnosis

 

Key clinical features:

 

  • Elderly, hypermetropic (farsighted) woman → anatomically predisposed (shallow anterior chamber).
  • Sudden onset of:
    • Severe ocular pain and redness
    • Blurred vision, halos around lights
    • Nausea and vomiting (due to vagal stimulation)
  • Exam findings:
    • Cloudy cornea (from corneal edema)
    • Mid-dilated, fixed, vertically oval pupil
    • Markedly raised intraocular pressure (IOP) (often >40–50 mmHg)
    • No fundus view due to corneal edema

 

All of these confirm acute primary angle-closure glaucoma.

 

Step 2 – Immediate (Emergency) Treatment

 

Goal: Rapidly reduce intraocular pressure (IOP) to prevent permanent optic nerve damage.

 

Immediate measures:

 

  1. Intravenous Acetazolamide (500 mg) – carbonic anhydrase inhibitor
    → Decreases aqueous humor production and rapidly lowers IOP.
  2. Topical beta-blocker (e.g., timolol) – reduces aqueous production.
  3. Topical pilocarpine (after IOP control) – causes miosis to open the angle.
  4. Hyperosmotic agents (e.g., IV mannitol) – in severe cases.

 

Step 3 – Definitive Treatment

 

Once the acute attack is controlled and corneal clarity improves:

 

Definitive procedure:

 

  • Laser peripheral iridotomy (LPI) using Nd:YAG 1064 nm laser (preferred)
    → Creates a small hole in the peripheral iris, allowing aqueous to flow directly from posterior to anterior chamber, relieving pupillary block.
    → Usually performed bilaterally since the other eye is at risk.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Topical pilocarpine and Nd:YAG 532 nm laser capsulotomy:

 

  • Capsulotomy is for posterior capsule opacification after cataract surgery, not for glaucoma.
  • Pilocarpine should be given after IOP reduction, not as an initial step when the iris is ischemic.

 

Option B. Intravenous Acetazolamide and Femtosecond laser iridotomy:

 

  • Femtosecond laser is used in refractive or cataract surgery, not standard for angle-closure management.

 

Option D. Topical Beta-Blockers and Trabeculectomy:

 

  • Trabeculectomy is a surgical procedure for chronic glaucoma, not the acute form.

This 60-year-old man presents 2 weeks after cataract surgery with marked visual loss, anterior chamber cells, and vitreous haze—with no fundus view.


This clinical picture is classic for postoperative endophthalmitis, an emergency intraocular infection.

 

Postoperative Endophthalmitis Definition:


Endophthalmitis is a severe inflammation/infection of the intraocular cavities (aqueous + vitreous), usually due to bacterial contamination during or after intraocular surgery.

 

Timing:

 

  • Acute form: Within 6 weeks of surgery (typically 1–2 weeks).
  • Chronic/delayed form: After 6 weeks

 

Causative Organisms:

 

A. Acute postoperative endophthalmitis:

 

  • Most common organism:Staphylococcus epidermidis (coagulase-negative staphylococcus)
  • Others: Staphylococcus aureus, Streptococcus species, Pseudomonas aeruginosa (fulminant course)

 

B. Delayed (chronic) postoperative endophthalmitis:

 

  • Propionibacterium acnes (now Cutibacterium acnes)
  • Presents weeks–months later, with milder inflammation.

 

Hence, in this case (2 weeks post-op, acute course), the most likely organism is Staphylococcus species.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Toxic anterior segment syndrome (TASS):

 

  • Sterile postoperative inflammation caused by toxic chemicals (e.g., detergents, preservatives).
  • Occurs within 12–48 hours after surgery, not 2 weeks later.
  • No organism involved, resolves with steroids.

 

Option B. Endophthalmitis; Propionibacterium cutis:

 

  • Propionibacterium acnes (cutis) causes chronic delayed-onset endophthalmitis (6+ weeks post-surgery).
  • Presents more indolently, not acute as in this case.

 

Option D. Sympathetic ophthalmia; Mucormycosis:

 

  • Sympathetic ophthalmia = bilateral granulomatous uveitis after penetrating injury, not after cataract surgery.
  • Mucormycosis affects immunocompromised patients with rhino-orbital involvement, not this presentation.

questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Intorsion, abduction, depression

Ans. C) Intorsion, abduction, depression 

 

The structure labeled A in the image corresponds to the Trochlear nerve (Cranial Nerve IV) — the only cranial nerve that emerges dorsally from the brainstem and innervates a single extraocular muscle: the Superior Oblique muscle.

 

Muscle Supplied:

 

Superior Oblique muscle

 

Nerve supply:


→ Trochlear nerve (CN IV)

 

Actions of the Superior Oblique Muscle:

 

  1. Primary action – Intorsion (medial rotation)
    • Rotates the top of the eyeball toward the nose.
    • Due to its insertion behind the equator of the eyeball.
  2. Secondary action – Depression
    • When the eye is adducted, the superior oblique acts as a depressor.
    • This distinguishes it from the inferior rectus, which depresses the abducted eye.
  3. Tertiary action – Abduction
    • Slightly moves the eye laterally, as the tendon passes through the trochlea to the superior posterolateral aspect of the globe.

 

Summary Table: [SIN RAD-mnemonic]

 

 

Mnemonic:

 

SO4 LR6 O3

 

  • SO (Superior Oblique) → CN IV (Trochlear)
  • LR (Lateral Rectus) → CN VI (Abducens)
  • All others → CN III (Oculomotor)

questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Drooping of the left eyelid

Ans. B) Drooping of the left eyelid

 

1. Interpreting the pupillary findings

 

  • Light in right eye → right pupil constricts (direct) but left pupil does not constrict (no consensual response).
  • Light in left eye → right pupil constricts (consensual) but left pupil does not constrict (no direct response).

 

This pattern means:

 

  • The afferent limb (optic nerve, CN II) is intact in both eyes, because shining light in either eye produces some pupillary constriction (in the right eye).
  • The efferent limb (oculomotor nerve, CN III) to the left eye is damaged, because the left pupil never constricts.

 

Thus, the lesion is an efferent (parasympathetic) defect of the left oculomotor nerve.

 

Left CN III palsy leads to:

 

  • Ptosis (levator palpebrae paralysis)
  • "Down and out" eye position (unopposed lateral rectus and superior oblique action)
  • Dilated pupil and loss of light reflex (sphincter pupillae paralysis)
  • Diplopia due to misalignment

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Absence of the left corneal reflex:

 

  • The afferent limb of the corneal reflex is trigeminal nerve (ophthalmic division, V1).
  • The efferent limb is facial nerve (VII) for eyelid closure.
  • CN III is not involved in this reflex.
    → So this would not occur in an oculomotor nerve lesion.

 

Option C. Inability to close the left eye:

 

  • Controlled by orbicularis oculi muscle (supplied by facial nerve, CN VII).
  • In CN III palsy, the eye cannot open fully (ptosis), not close.
    → So this suggests a facial nerve lesion, not oculomotor.

 

Option D. Inward deviation of the left eye:

 

  • An inwardly deviated (esotropic) eye occurs in abducens (CN VI) palsy**, due to loss of the lateral rectus muscle.
  • In CN III palsy, the eye is outwardly deviated (exotropic) due to unopposed action of the lateral rectus and superior oblique.

questions.text: Which of the following can‍ occur in a patient with ​prolactinoma?
questions.raw_text: Which of the following can occur in a patient with prolactinoma?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Superior quadrantanopia

Ans. A) Superior quadrantanopia

 

  • Prolactinomas are pituitary tumors which can grow large enough (macroprolactinomas) to compress the optic chiasm, located just above the sella turcica.
  • The optic chiasm anatomy with crossing fibers is organized such that the inferior retinal fibers (which receive superior visual field information) cross in the anterior chiasm.
  • Compression of the inferior fibers in the optic chiasm may result in superior visual field defects, including superior quadrantanopia. This is less common than the classic bitemporal hemianopia but can occur depending on tumor location and chiasmal anatomy.
  • Visual field defects from prolactinomas are usually bitemporal hemianopias but can vary in pattern.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Inferior quadrantanopia:

 

  • Inferior quadrantanopia usually results from lesions further back in the visual pathway, especially the temporal lobe (Meyer's loop) or parietal lobe.
  • It is not a typical finding in prolactinoma because these tumours do not compress these posterior visual pathways.

 

Option C. Priapism:

 

  • Priapism (prolonged painful erection) is not a typical feature associated with prolactinoma.
  • Prolactinomas often cause hypogonadism via prolactin-induced inhibition of gonadotropin-releasing hormone, leading to decreased libido and erectile dysfunction, the opposite effect of priapism.

 

Option D. Failure of lactation:

 

  • Prolactin is the hormone responsible for stimulating milk production.
  • Prolactinomas cause elevated prolactin levels leading to galactorrhoea and sometimes inappropriate lactation or failure of lactation due to disrupted hormonal balance.
  • However, the term "failure of lactation" is usually not associated with prolactinoma; instead, excess prolactin causes milk production outside of pregnancy or lactation.

Ans. D) Congenital glaucoma

PHPV (also called Persistent Fetal Vasculature) is due to failure of regression of the fetal hyaloid vascular system.


It presents as unilateral leukocoria in an otherwise full-term infant with normal birth history.


Ultrasound or MRI shows a retrolental mass with a stalk from optic disc to lens.

 

Option C. Retinopathy of Prematurity (ROP): Possible.
ROP occurs in premature infants (<32 weeks or <1500 g) who receive high oxygen therapy.


It leads to fibrovascular proliferation and retinal detachment, appearing as leukocoria in advanced stages.


Hence, it is a valid differential in premature infants

Correct answer: D. Strabismus surgery

Ans. D) Strabismus surgery

 

Strabismus surgery is not a primary treatment for amblyopia itself — it corrects ocular alignment, but does not improve the amblyopic eye’s visual acuity.


If performed before proper visual stimulation therapy (like patching or penalization), the amblyopia may persist even after alignment.


Hence, amblyopia must be treated first (with patching and vision therapy), and strabismus surgery is done later for cosmetic and binocular alignment purposes.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Patching: Correct Management.


Patching (occlusion therapy) involves covering the better eye to force use of the amblyopic (lazy) eye.


It stimulates visual cortex development and is the mainstay of amblyopia therapy.


Usually prescribed for 2–6 hours/day depending on severity and age.

 

Option B. Video games: Correct Management.


Special interactive video games and visual training programs help improve fixation and contrast sensitivity in the amblyopic eye.


These stimulate binocular cooperation and are used as an adjunct to traditional patching therapy.


They enhance compliance and neurovisual adaptation.

 

Option C. Refractive error correction: Correct Management.


Refractive correction using appropriate glasses or contact lenses is the first step in amblyopia management.


In anisometropic amblyopia, correcting the refractive difference alone can significantly improve vision.


Sometimes full correction for 4–6 weeks precedes patching therapy.

Ans. C) Purtscher’s retinopathy

 

Purtscher’s retinopathy is a microvascular occlusive retinopathy associated with acute pancreatitis, chest compression injury, long bone fractures, or other severe systemic trauma.
It usually develops within 24–48 hours after the inciting event.

 

Typical Fundus Findings:

 

  • Purtscher flecken: polygonal, well-defined areas of retinal whitening between arterioles and venules.
  • Cotton wool spots: due to focal infarction of nerve fiber layer.
  • Retinal hemorrhages: usually few, around the posterior pole.
  • Macula may show edema → decreased vision.

 

Pathophysiology:


Complement activation → leukocyte aggregation → precapillary arteriolar occlusion → ischemia of the retina.

 

Hence, a patient developing these findings after acute pancreatitis or trauma is classic for Purtscher’s retinopathy.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Hypertensive retinopathy: Incorrect.

 

  • Occurs in long-standing hypertension, not acutely after abdominal pain.
  • Shows arteriolar narrowing, A-V nicking, flame-shaped hemorrhages, and hard exudates forming a macular star.
  • No temporal relationship with pancreatitis or trauma.

 

Option B. Diabetic retinopathy: Incorrect.

 

  • A chronic microangiopathy seen in diabetics.
  • Fundus shows microaneurysms, dot and blot hemorrhages, hard exudates, and neovascularization.
  • Not associated with sudden systemic events like acute pancreatitis.

 

Option D. Central retinal vein occlusion (CRVO): Incorrect.

 

  • Presents with sudden painless vision loss.
  • Fundus shows “blood and thunder” appearance: widespread hemorrhages, dilated tortuous veins, and cotton wool spots.
  • Unlike Purtscher’s, it is unilateral and not associated with trauma or pancreatitis

questions.raw_text:
In optic neuritis, which of the following statements is true?


1.    70% patients of multiple sclerosis present with optic neuritis
2.    Oral steroids are an appropriate treatment
3.    It can have a normal fundus with no disc edema
4.    Colour vision and contrast are proportionally affected to vision impairment
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 3 only

Ans. D) 3 only

 

It can have a normal fundus with no disc edema: True.
In retrobulbar optic neuritis, inflammation involves the optic nerve posterior to the globe, so the optic disc appears normal initially (“the patient sees nothing, and the doctor sees nothing”).


Only later, mild pallor may appear as optic atrophy sets in.

 

Hence, a normal fundus despite significant vision loss is typical of optic neuritis.

 

Incorrect Statements:

 

1. 70% patients of multiple sclerosis present with optic neuritis – False.


This is reversed:
→ About 50% of patients with optic neuritis later develop multiple sclerosis (MS) within 15 years.
However, only about 20–25% of MS patients present initially with optic neuritis — not 70%.
Thus, this statement is incorrect.

 

2. Oral steroids are an appropriate treatment – False.


High-dose intravenous methylprednisolone (IVMP) is the treatment of choice, as shown by the Optic Neuritis Treatment Trial (ONTT).
Oral steroids alone (without IV phase) are contraindicated — they increase recurrence risk and delay recovery.
Therefore, oral steroids alone are inappropriate.

 

4. Colour vision and contrast are proportionally affected to vision impairment – False.


In optic neuritis, colour vision and contrast sensitivity are disproportionately affected, often more severely than visual acuity.
Patients may have marked dyschromatopsia even when Snellen acuity is near normal.


Hence, this statement is incorrect.

The image shows ptosis, miosis, and apparent enophthalmos on one side — the classic triad of Horner’s syndrome.


The question also mentions unilateral facial anhidrosis, confirming sympathetic pathway disruption.

 

Sympathetic Pathway to the Eye

 

  1. First-order neuron (Central):
    • Originates in the hypothalamus → descends to ciliospinal center of Budge (C8–T2).
  2. Second-order neuron (Preganglionic):
    • From T1 level, exits spinal cord through white ramus communicans, then ascends in the sympathetic chain to superior cervical ganglion.
  3. Third-order neuron (Postganglionic):
    • From superior cervical ganglion → along internal carotid artery → cavernous sinus → joins ophthalmic division of CN V → supplies dilator pupillae and Müller’s muscle.

 

Lesion Site Analysis

 

  • Lesion at white ramus of T1 (preganglionic fiber) → interrupts sympathetic outflow to:
    • Eye → causes ptosis, miosis
    • Face → causes anhidrosis (since sweat fibers to face arise at this level)

 

Thus, white ramus of T1 lesion produces complete Horner’s syndrome with facial anhidrosis, matching the question.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Grey ramus of T1: Incorrect.

 

  • Grey ramus carries postganglionic fibers returning to spinal nerves for body wall sweat glands.
  • Does not supply the face, so lesion here wouldn’t produce ocular findings.

 

Option B. Grey ramus of C8: Incorrect.

 

  • Similar reasoning — not part of ocular sympathetic pathway.
  • C8 fibers mainly supply upper limb, not the face or eye.

 

Option D. White ramus of C8: Incorrect.

 

  • C8 does not carry sympathetic fibers to the eye; T1 is the key segment for ocular sympathetic outflow.
  • Therefore, lesion at C8 would not produce Horner’s syndrome.

  • Involves making radial corneal incisions that cause corneal flattening.
  • Corrects low-to-moderate myopia (−2 to −6 D).

  • Implantation of PMMA semicircular rings in the peripheral corneal stroma.

Suprachoroidal hemorrhage does not lead to hypotonic maculopathy because it typically causes an increase in intraocular pressure, not a decrease.
